title: Preface
summary: Front matter of a August 3, 1977 joint hearing before the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the Subcommittee on Health and Scientific Research, on Project MKULTRA, the CIA's program of research in behavioral modification. Printed by the U.S. Government Printing Office, 1977.

title: SENATE SELECT COMMITTEE ON INTELLIGENCE
summary: Front matter of a 1970s-era U.S. Senate document listing members of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (Chairman Daniel K. Inouye, Vice Chairman Barry Goldwater, plus members and staff) and the Committee on Human Resources (Chairman Harrison A. Williams Jr., members, and staff), including the Subcommittee on Health and Scientific Research (Chairman Edward M. Kennedy) and its professional and minority staff. No substantive content beyond the membership rosters and staff assignments.

title: CONTESTS

nodes.title: CONTESTS (intro)
CONTESTS (intro)
nodes.summary: Table of contents for a 1977 Senate hearing on CIA Project MKULTRA, the agency's behavioral modification research program, listing witness statements (Admiral Stansfield Turner and CIA officials; former employees Philip Goldman and John Gittinger), appendices on chemical and biological agent testing, MKULTRA documents and subprojects, and material on psychological assessments, truth drugs, drug testing abroad, and related projects. The opening remarks by Senators Inouye and Kennedy describe the hearing's purpose: examining newly discovered records of CIA human experimentation, including covert drug tests on unwitting citizens, university involvement, a death, and the 1973 destruction of records. They call for oversight, notification of affected institutions, and expanded protections for human subjects research.

nodes.title: PREPARED STATEMENT OF ADMIRAL STANSFIELD TURNER, DIRECTOR OF CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE
nodes.summary: Director of Central Intelligence Stansfield Turner's 1977 statement on Project MKULTRA, a CIA program (1953-1964) funding behavioral modification and drug research, including the 1953 death of Dr. Frank Olson after unwitting LSD dosing. It explains that seven boxes of finance folders were recently found at a records center after earlier searches missed them, describes their contents (149 subprojects, cut-out funding audits, 33 unrelated intelligence subprojects), and notes the 1963 Inspector General report and the 1973 file destruction.

Introduces a 1977 Senate hearing on CIA Project MKULTRA, the agency's behavioral modification and drug research program. Covers statements by Admiral Stansfield Turner and former employees Philip Goldman and John Gittinger, and appendices on agent testing and subprojects. Senators Inouye and Kennedy urge oversight of newly found records of CIA experiments on unwitting citizens, including a death and the 1973 records destruction. Turner's statement details the program (1953-1964), Frank Olson's death after LSD dosing, seven boxes of recovered finance folders, and the 1963 Inspector General report.

nodes.title: 1. Research into the effects of behavioral drugs and/or alcohol:
nodes.summary: The text covers CIA Project MKULTRA (1953–1964), a program of drug and behavioral modification research. It details 149 subprojects by category: drug effects (some involving unwitting human subjects), hypnosis, chemical acquisition, magic-based covert techniques, behavioral studies, polygraph work, funding mechanisms, biological/toxin research, and Fort Detrick support. Newly recovered records name 185 researchers and 80 institutions, and reveal a $375,000 CIA donation routed through an intermediary to a medical institution, plus safehouse unwitting drug testing in San Francisco and New York. Admiral Turner's testimony explains the records' late discovery, the 1973 destruction, and CIA assurances of no current testing. Senators question oversight, the donation, and CIA psychological assessments. The text also includes a 1950s excerpt on 'truth serum' drugs such as scopolamine in interrogation.

nodes.title: THE BARBITURATES
nodes.summary: Barbiturates history and use: accidental 1916 discovery of drug-facilitated communication with a catatonic patient; 1930s psychiatric adjunct experiments; police use for interrogation, with Muehlberger using them by 1935 though courts rejected drug-induced confessions. Barbiturates, synthesized 1903, are versatile depressants with billions of doses prescribed yearly in the US under many names. Sodium amytal, pentothal, and seconal serve as truth drugs. Intravenous use produces stages of drunkenness over minutes: sedation, unconsciousness, deep narcosis, death. Plane 3 is the psychiatric work stage.

nodes.title: CLINICAL AND EXPERIMENTAL STUDIES
CLINICAL AND EXPERIMENTAL STUDIES (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers Western reluctance to study drugs for interrogation and a review of experiments on drug-aided confessions. Gerson and Victoroff used amytal interviews on 17 neuropsychiatric soldiers, finding confessions unreliable (fantasy, lost time-sense, retractions; 8 of 9 retracted). Redlich et al. at Yale showed barbiturate-influenced subjects could keep cover stories, while neurotics confessed more easily. Stimulants (methedrine) claims by Brussel and Gottschalk's critique are noted; combined barbiturate-stimulant-tranquilizer use merits further study.

nodes.title: OBSERVATIONS FROM PRACTICE
nodes.summary: Drug interrogation (narcoanalysis) is of doubtful value for obtaining confessions. Psychopaths resist drugs and can feign amnesia or falsely confess. MacDonald, Freedman, and Inbau find drugs reveal psychiatrically useful but unreliable information and rarely expose deception. Grinker and Spiegel found non-drug therapy yields the same material given time. Drugs give fast access to psychologically useful but not necessarily true information; skilled interrogation or therapy can get better truth.

nodes.title: APPLICATION TO CI INTERROGATION
nodes.summary: Discusses applying 'truth' drugs (narcoanalysis) to intelligence interrogation. Covers limited evidence, drugs as an aid to skilled interrogators, heightened suggestibility, and the role of trust and rapport, including role-play. Notes subjects feel they revealed more than they did, placebo effects, hypnosis limits, and defenses: avoiding drugs, 'dry run' trials, barbiturate addiction risk, and hallucinogens like LSD. Concludes resistance rests on the individual's emotional stability.

Reviews Western clinical and experimental work on drug-aided interrogation (narcoanalysis). Gerson and Victoroff found amytal-elicited confessions unreliable (8 of 9 retracted); Redlich et al. showed barbiturate subjects could keep cover stories; stimulant claims and combined-drug use need study. Practice observations: drugs yield psychologically useful but unreliable information, psychopaths resist, and non-drug therapy gets similar material given time. For intelligence use: drugs aid skilled interrogators, raise suggestibility, depend on rapport, risk placebo effects and addiction, and resistance depends on emotional stability.

nodes.title: CONCLUSIONS
nodes.summary: No true truth serum exists. Barbiturates may aid interrogation by disrupting defenses, but their output is contaminated by deception, fantasy, and garbled speech, and subjects tend to overbelieve what they revealed. Normal individuals and psychopaths can resist drug interrogation, and anyone who withstands intensive interrogation can likely hold out under narcosis. Foreknowledge of the process and its limits is the best defense. Controlled experimental studies of depressants, stimulants, their combinations, and ataraxics are urgently needed.

nodes.title: REFERENCES
REFERENCES (intro)
nodes.summary: The text is a reference list of about 29 works on drug-induced truth serums, narcoanalysis, barbiturates, scopolamine, LSD, and hypnosis in interrogation, spanning 1922 to 1960. It is followed by Senate hearing testimony (circa 1977) from Admiral Turner, CIA Director, on the MKULTRA program. Senators Wallop, Chafee, Inouye, Goldwater, Kennedy, Schweiker, and Huddleston question him on unwitting drug experiments on civilians, safe houses in San Francisco and New York, the Frank Olson death, a Georgetown hospital wing, and concussion weapons research (Subprojects 45, 54). Topics include notifying victims and universities, the whereabouts of Dr. Gottlieb, and oversight reforms. The text ends with Philip Goldman and John Gittinger being sworn in as former CIA employees, with Goldman disputing his listed role as monitor.

nodes.title: TESTIMONY OF JOHN GITTINGER, FORMER EMPLOYEE,CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY
nodes.summary: Transcript of a 1970s Senate hearing on CIA MKULTRA. Senator Kennedy questions former CIA employees John Goldman, a project officer who disbursed funds for San Francisco and New York safe houses, and John Gittinger, a psychologist. Topics include unwitting LSD and drug testing, prostitutes used in safe-house interviews, two-way mirrors, the Society for the Investigation of Human Ecology funding university research, and the Psychological Assessments Foundation. Senators Case and Schweiker ask about foreign university funding and brainwashing. Inouye notes the witnesses appeared voluntarily, then the hearing recesses.

A reference list of about 29 works (1922-1960) on drug-induced truth serums, narcoanalysis, barbiturates, scopolamine, LSD, and hypnosis in interrogation. Followed by 1970s Senate testimony on the CIA MKULTRA program: unwitting drug experiments on civilians, San Francisco and New York safe houses, the Frank Olson death, a Georgetown hospital wing, concussion weapons research, victim and university notification, oversight reforms, and testimony from former employees Philip Goldman and John Gittinger on funding, safe-house interviews, and foreign university research.

summary: Introduces a 1977 Senate hearing on CIA MKULTRA, a 1953-1964 behavioral drug research program. Covers Admiral Turner's testimony, former employees' statements, the Frank Olson LSD death, 1973 records destruction, and recovered files naming 185 researchers and 80 institutions, including a $375,000 donation and unwitting safehouse testing. Also covers barbiturate history, narcoanalysis studies finding drug confessions unreliable, conclusions that no true truth serum exists, and a reference list.

title: APPENDIX A

nodes.title: APPENDIX A (intro)
nodes.summary: Senate Select Committee section on CIA and military intelligence chemical and biological agent testing. Covers the defensive origins that shifted to offensive behavior-altering research in the late 1940s-50s, covert tests on unwitting subjects, and few records kept. Describes resulting rights abridgments, two American deaths, and the Blauer death (1953). Notes waived CIA administrative controls, compartmentation, and failed inter-agency cooperation, including the Army concealing its LSD testing from the CIA. Raises questions about command and control, foreign complicity, and the use of institutions as cover.

nodes.title: A. THE PROGRAMS INVESTIGATED
1. Project CHATTER
nodes.summary: Describes Project CHATTER, a Navy program started in fall 1947 that investigated 'truth drugs' after reports of Soviet success. It tested substances (Anabasis aphylla, scopolamine, mescaline) for speech-inducing effects via lab experiments on animals and human subjects, included overseas experiments, expanded during the Korean War, and ended around 1953.

nodes.title: 2. Project BLUEBIRD/ARTICHOKE
nodes.summary: Covers CIA Project BLUEBIRD (1950), approved by the Director to find ways to condition personnel against information extraction, investigate control via interrogation, enhance memory, and build defenses against hostile control; added offensive interrogation evaluation (hypnosis, drugs). Renamed ARTICHOKE in 1951, with in-house experiments and overseas sodium pentothal/hypnosis interrogations. OSI led it initially; in 1952 responsibility moved to the Inspection and Security Office, shifting focus to operational use of hypnosis and truth serums. CIA says it ended in 1956, but evidence suggests special interrogation continued after 1953.

nodes.title: 3. IKNAOMI
nodes.summary: Describes CIA program MKNAOMI (1967 objectives: covert support base, stockpiling incapacitating and lethal materials for Technical Services Division, maintaining biological/chemical dissemination items, surveillance and testing). Covers the 1952 CIA-Army agreement with Fort Detrick's Special Operations Division, which developed biological darts, pills, a dog-incapacitating gun, and crop/animal attack methods. MKNAOMI ended in 1970 after Nixon's 1969-1970 renunciation of biological weapons and toxin destruction orders, though a CIA scientist secretly kept 11 grams of shellfish toxin.

nodes.title: 4. MKULTRA
nodes.summary: Describes the CIA's MKULTRA program, a 1950s-60s effort researching chemical and biological agents to control human behavior. Covers its 1953 approval under Helms, the 1973 destruction of records, the three research phases (material search, testing on volunteers and unwitting subjects, field application), LSD testing via the Bureau of Narcotics, MKDELTA overseas use, interrogation and harassment applications, and the 1963 Inspector General discovery that halted unwitting testing and led to tighter controls.

nodes.title: 5. The Testing of LSD by the Army
B. CIA DRUG TESTING PROGRAMS
nodes.summary: Describes the CIA and Army LSD testing programs of the 1950s. Army testing had three phases: volunteer soldiers in chemical warfare experiments, Material Testing Program EA 1729 with 95 volunteers, and Projects THIRD CHANCE and DERBY HAT with 16 unwitting subjects. CIA programs arose from Cold War fears of Soviet and Chinese chemical/biological weapons, shifting from defensive to offensive aims, including covert LSD dosing of nonvolunteers. These were concealed from the executive branch, Congress, and the public. The text ends with the 1953 death of Dr. Frank Olson after he was unwittingly dosed with LSD.

nodes.title: a. Background.
nodes.summary: Background on Dr. Olson, an aerobiology expert in the Army's Special Operations Division at Camp Detrick, which assessed US vulnerability to biological attack, developed offensive biological weapon techniques, and conducted biological research for the CIA. Colleagues, including Colonel Ruwet and Dr. Lashbrook, described him as professional and perfectly normal before he received LSD. This contradicts later CIA internal memos assessing his emotional stability after his death.

nodes.title: b. The Experiment.
nodes.summary: Describes a November 1953 CIA and Camp Detrick conference at Deep Creek Lake, Maryland, where participants reportedly agreed an unwitting LSD experiment was desirable, contrary to Vincent Ruwet's recollection. It notes Richard Helms's May 1953 warning about LSD and Frank Wisner's memo requiring DDP approval, neither of which specifically authorized the experiment. Gottlieb had LSD secretly placed in Cointreau served to Special Operations Division staff, including Dr. Olson, causing boisterousness, sleeplessness, and agitation the next morning.

nodes.title: c. The Treatment.
nodes.summary: Describes the Olson case from the 1953 CIA LSD affair: Olson's depression after the Nov. 1953 LSD exposure, Ruwet and Lashbrook arranging medical help, consultations with Dr. Harold Abramson in New York, and Olson's return to Washington and family. Also covers Gottlieb's testimony that LSD seemed benign, Beecher's warning memo on LSD research dangers, and a cited Geneva suicide case that Rothland failed to disclose.

nodes.title: d. The Death.
nodes.summary: Lashbrook and Olson, after failing to get a Friday flight, checked into the Statler Hotel and spent the evening watching TV, drinking, and dining; Olson seemed cheerful and relaxed. At about 2:30 a.m. Saturday, November 28, Lashbrook was woken by breaking glass and found Olson had jumped from their 10th-floor window to his death. Lashbrook then notified Gottlieb, Ruwet, Abramson, the hotel, and police, telling police Olson had ulcers.

nodes.title: e. The Aftermath.
nodes.summary: Describes CIA handling of Dr. Olson's death from an unwitting drug experiment: the CIA paid death benefits without disclosing circumstances, concealed the CIA link via cover for Lashbrook, and ran an internal probe. The General Counsel called the experiment culpable negligence. DCI Dulles sent critical letters to the TSS Chief and Dr. Gottlieb, which were explicitly not reprimands, with no personnel file notes and no effect on careers.

nodes.title: 3. The Surreptitious Administration of LSD to Unwitting Non-Volunteer Human Subjects by the CIA After the Death of Dr. Olson
nodes.summary: Describes the CIA's 1950s-1963 MKULTRA program of surreptitiously administering LSD to unwitting non-volunteer US subjects after Dr. Olson's death, including dangers, lack of consent, medical safeguards, and follow-up; Director criticism of TSS officers; Helms' memos arguing unwitting testing was necessary; the 1963 halt after an Inspector General survey; continued debate and no disciplinary action; and an introduction to CIA failures in monitoring chemical and biological agent testing.

nodes.title: a. The Waiver of Administrative Control.
nodes.summary: Describes CIA MKULTRA chemical and biological agent research waivers of normal administrative controls. Helms ordered destruction of program documents in 1973 via CSI 70-10 waiver, hindering the Committee's inquiry and victim medical aid. MKULTRA was started in 1953 with unwritten contracts, unaudited funds, and unclear lines of authority; the Inspector General and Audit Branch found deficiencies. MKNAOMI at Fort Detrick kept no transfer records of agents like anthrax, leaving the Agency unable to track materials.

nodes.title: b. Authorization.
nodes.summary: Covers CIA MKULTRA program authorization problems: destroyed documents and no records of approval, Dulles authorized the program but records are unclear on specific projects like unwitting LSD testing. McCone was apparently not briefed in detail, and deputies were not briefed. Authorization by lack of disagreement was common for sensitive projects. Shellfish toxin retention violated orders, LSD experiment proceeded without notifying superiors, and chemical-agent approvals excluded the medical staff. BNDD coordination and Commissioner Anslinger's and Giordano's knowledge are uncertain. The CIA was reluctant to share information with Congress.

nodes.title: c. Internal Review.
nodes.summary: Describes internal review failures in CIA MKULTRA and related programs: waived regulations and sparse documentation weakened oversight. The General Counsel and Inspector General were excluded from reviewing the covert LSD project, which the 1957 IG survey missed and an inspector found only in 1963. The Audit Staff faced difficulty verifying contractor accounts. Compartmentation and jurisdictional conflict among TSD, Office of Medical Services, and Office of Security hindered information sharing via BLUEBIRD, ARTICHOKE, and QKHILLTOP, and affected policymaking, including a 1958 DDP committee.

The section covers the Army's 1950s LSD testing (volunteer chemical warfare experiments, Material Testing Program EA 1729 with 95 volunteers, and Projects THIRD CHANCE and DERBY HAT with 16 unwitting subjects) and parallel CIA programs driven by Cold War fears, including covert dosing. It details Dr. Frank Olson's unwitting 1953 LSD dosing, his death, and the CIA's aftermath response. It then addresses MKULTRA's continued unwitting LSD testing until 1963, administrative waivers, weak authorization and internal review, and compartmentation hindering oversight.

Covers the CIA and Navy programs investigated: Project CHATTER (1947-1953, Navy truth-drug research), BLUEBIRD/ARTICHOKE (1950s interrogation and hypnosis work, possibly continuing past 1953), MKNAOMI (biological and chemical weapons stockpiling, ended 1970 after Nixon's renunciation), and MKULTRA (1953-1960s mind-control research, halted unwitting testing in 1963). Also covers Army LSD testing, including Dr. Frank Olson's 1953 unwitting dosing and death, and oversight failures.

nodes.title: C. COVERT TESTING ON HUMAN SUBJECTS BY MILITARY INTELLIGENCE
C. COVERT TESTING ON HUMAN SUBJECTS BY MILITARY INTELLIGENCE (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the Army's covert LSD testing on unwitting humans under Material Testing Program EA 1729, including Projects THIRD CHANCE and DERBY HAT in Europe and the Far East. Motivated by suspected Soviet interest in LSD and counterintelligence concerns, the tests mirrored CIA programs, neglecting informed consent, follow-up exams, and secrecy-driven rights, with unclear authorization and supervision.

nodes.title: 1. Scope of Testing
nodes.summary: Describes the 1955-1958 Army Chemical Corps research testing LSD as a chemical warfare incapacitating agent on over 1,000 volunteers, mostly at Edgewood, Maryland. In 1958 intelligence-potential tests on 95 volunteers under Material Testing Program EA 1729 used three structured experiments: surreptitious dosing at a social reception, polygraphed subjects, and isolation chambers. Field tests followed: Project THIRDCHANCE (Europe, 1961, ten non-volunteers, one showing severe paranoia) and Project DERBY HAT (Far East, 1962, seven foreign nationals).

nodes.title: 2. Inadequate CoordinationAmong IntelligenceAgencies
nodes.summary: The text covers flaws in the U.S. Army's LSD testing program (EA 1729, Project THIRD CHANCE and DERBY HAT). It details: the 1959 USAINTC staff study that downplayed LSD risks despite an unexamined prior death; inadequate coordination with the CIA and FBI, with planners postponing it; a 1961 interrogation of a U.S. soldier and tactics used on drugged subjects; a 1962 Far East case where a suspect was dosed and interrogated for hours; the study's legal and moral dismissals; and flawed consent and security forms that hid risks and barred seeking medical help. It concludes the program was not truly voluntary and lacked long-term medical care.

nodes.title: 4. Lack ofNormal Authorization and Supervision
nodes.summary: The Army's LSD testing programs operated under informal, inadequate authorization, violating its own procedures. The May 1955/1956 field station plan lacked the required Secretary of the Army approval. Later Edgewood testing (EA 1729) was approved only at intelligence board level, not by the Surgeon General. THIRD CHANCE and DERBY HAT operational LSD projects got verbal ACSI approval in December 1960, with written approval only in January 1961 and no Secretary knowledge. General Wheeler received the THIRD CHANCE trip report in 1963, likely reading only conclusions.

nodes.title: 5. Terminationof Te8ting
nodes.summary: Covers the April 1963 briefing on Projects THIRD CHANCE and DERBY HAT, which concluded more field testing was needed before LSD could aid counterintelligence interrogations; the Deputy ACSI ordered no further field testing. The ACSI then asked the CDC to review the projects and revise FM 30-17 so drug use in interrogations requires prior Department of the Army approval, citing unreliable results and moral, legal, medical, and political problems. This effectively ended Army LSD field testing, with a September 1963 meeting suspending the program.

Covers the Army's covert LSD testing on unwitting subjects under Material Testing Program EA 1729 (Projects THIRD CHANCE in Europe and DERBY HAT in the Far East), driven by Soviet-LSD and counterintelligence concerns. Testing on over 1,000 volunteers (1955-58) and field tests on non-volunteers were marked by inadequate consent, medical follow-up, coordination with CIA/FBI, and authorization, which ran informally and violated Army procedures. Operations were approved verbally, then in writing, without Secretary knowledge. The 1963 review ended field testing and required prior Department of the Army approval for drug use in interrogations.

nodes.title: D. COOPERATION AND COMPETITION AMONG THE INTELLIGENCE COM-
nodes.summary: Covers cooperation and competition among CIA, military, FBI and other intelligence agencies in MKULTRA-era chemical/biological and LSD testing: early cooperation breaking down, Project THIRD CHANCE and MKNAOMI information failures, and CIA attempts to spy on military programs. Also covers foreign liaison services, including interrogation-subject testing and research abroad that may evade U.S. law. Covers the Bureau of Narcotics cut-out arrangement and its command-and-control problems, and outside institutions and individuals (universities, hospitals, prisons) used without informed consent. Raises classification and secrecy concerns.

summary: Senate Select Committee review of CIA and military chemical/biological and behavior-altering agent testing, 1947-1970s. Covers the programs (CHATTER, BLUEBIRD/ARTICHOKE, MKNAOMI, MKULTRA, Army LSD testing including Frank Olson's 1953 death), covert tests on unwitting subjects, the Army's EA 1729 field tests, waived controls, inter-agency competition, foreign and institutional involvement, and classification and oversight failures.

title: APPENDIX B
summary: A 1977 memo from David S. Brandwein (Office of Technical Service) to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence reports newly located MKULTRA documents, found in retired OTS Budget and Fiscal records after earlier searches missed them. The subproject files contain mostly proposals and memoranda, with a possibly controversial $35,000 contribution routed through a private donation mechanism to match federal funds. Key points: a knockout drug research project tied to cancer work at a university, the Marks FOIA litigation timeline, and a recommendation to release sanitized material to Marks' attorneys and inform the Senate Select Committee. A 1977 letter from DCI Stansfield Turner to Senator Daniel Inouye acknowledges MKULTRA tests on U.S. citizens without their knowledge, surreptitious drug administration, use of addicts and alcoholics as subjects, knockout drug research tied to cancer pain treatment with patient tests, and a possible improper payment to a private institution. Turner states the activities were discontinued over ten years earlier and offers testimony.

title: APPENDIX C
summary: A 1953 memorandum describing Project MKULTRA Subproject 2, which would provide secure, efficient support to the MKULTRA program via a psychiatrist-consultant with prior Chief Neuropsychiatrist and OSS experience. Scope: miscellaneous research/testing, serving as contact and cut-out for projects in the area, monitoring selected projects, and general consulting. Cost capped at $4,650 for one year. Includes TOP SECRET clearance note and approval signature lines.

title: PROPOSAL.
summary: A two-part proposal. (1) Objective: study synergistic effects of drug combinations suited to abolishing consciousness, since combinations (e.g., barbiturates) may be more effective yet hazardous, notably to respiration; animal experiments first. Requests $1000 for animal experiments, informal, without a specific grant. (2) Objective: study covert drug administration without patient knowledge, surveying criminal methods and psychodynamics, and preparing a manual; requests $1000 as needed. Document is a fragmentary scanned memo header.

title: SUBJC

nodes.title: SUBJC (intro)
nodes.summary: Subproject 2 is initiated to secure an efficient means of exploiting the NKUIMs program. It describes a practicing psychiatrist who serves as advisor and faculty member, plus consultant contacting individuals in the field, and conducts his own research. Duties include miscellaneous research and testing in the general field, serving as contact for projects in selected field areas, monitoring, general consultant and advisor, and medical advisor. He is reimbursed for services and expenses via invoice, with travel reimbursed under standard Government allowances. The text is partly garbled OCR.

nodes.title: Project MLTRA, Subproject 16
nodes.summary: Project MLTRA Subproject 16 continues Subproject 3, which set up facilities for realistic testing of R&D items for CD/TSS and APD/TSS. Subproject 16 funds continued maintenance because alterations, equipment, and initial supplies were underestimated. Conducted by a unit with support from CD/TSS and APD/TSS; estimated one-year cost $7,740.00. Remaining text is garbled OCR with a memo about payments via a cashier and suspicious banks.

nodes.title: Project ICULilRA, SubproJect 23
nodes.summary: Project ICULilRA, Subproject 23: consolidates in-house agency activities under CD/TISS into one general project, replacing three concluding projects. A consultant (Dr. ?) with Top Secret clearance will study materials, provides cover and cut-out facilities; one-year cost cap about $2,700. Research studies CNS-acting chemical agents: testing known and synthesized drugs on animals for acute/chronic toxicity, pharmacological assays, pathology, preliminary clinical trials, quarterly reports. Budget: personnel $30,700; other expenditures $12,000; total $42,700 (October 195T memorandum).

nodes.title: Increase in the Scope of Subproject 23, Project MKULTRA
nodes.summary: Increase in the Scope of Subproject 23, Project MKULTRA

summary: Subproject 2 (SUBJC) engages a practicing psychiatrist as advisor, faculty member, consultant, and researcher for miscellaneous field research, testing, monitoring, and medical advice, reimbursed by invoice with standard travel allowances. Project MLTRA Subproject 16 funds continued maintenance of testing facilities for CD/TSS and APD/TSS R&D, estimated at $7,740 for one year. Project ICULilRA Subproject 23 consolidates in-house activities under CD/TISS, uses a cleared consultant, and studies CNS-acting chemical agents through animal toxicity, pharmacology, pathology, and clinical trials, with a $42,700 budget. The final entry covers an increase in Subproject 23's scope.

title: SUBJECT:

nodes.title: SUBJECT: (intro)
nodes.summary: A 1955 CIA-related memo on Project MKULTRA Subproject 23 covering a $15,000 increase to the $42,700 obligation (total $57,700 through 28 January 1955) due to expanded TSS/CD direction and development of two new biologically active compounds. A 25 August 1955 memo requests authorization for $658.05 paid to hospital expenses of terminally ill cancer patients used for testing chemical effects on humans, with verbal approval from the chief. A 21 December 1954 memo to the Director of Central Intelligence on Subproject 35 is also included.

nodes.title: SUBJECT
nodes.summary: A 1955 CIA-era legal memo and related documents: the General Counsel finds a gift of Government funds to a hospital/individual permissible if it yields a valuable, unobtainable product with reasonable expectation of return; discusses control risks if the individual dies or becomes incapacitated, overhead charge avoidance due to the ostensible private source, and whether charitable funding was available. Also covers memos on a budget increase and a May 1955 TSS program listing covert drug-research objectives (incapacitating, truth-related, and interrogation-related substances, amnesia methods) and the need for private physicians to conduct human testing.

summary: Covers CIA-related Project MKULTRA memos from 1954-1955: a $15,000 increase to Subproject 23 (total $57,700) for expanded TSS/CD work and two new biologically active compounds; a request for $658.05 paid to hospitals for terminally ill cancer patients used in human chemical testing; a Subproject 35 memo to the DCI; a General Counsel opinion that gifts of Government funds are permissible if they yield unobtainable products, weighing control, overhead and charitable-funding risks; and a May 1955 TSS program listing covert drug-research goals (incapacitating, truth, interrogation substances, amnesia) needing private physicians.

title: SUBPROJECT 35 OF PROJECT MKULTRA
summary: Subproject 35 of MKULTRA: the DGI approved on 15 Jan 1955 a $125,000 CIA contribution toward a $3M research wing, giving the Agency one-sixth of the space for covert biological and chemical warfare research. The building fund was to combine donations, CIA money, and matching Public Law 221 funds. The Agency now requests an extra $250,000, raising its contribution to $375,000 (matched equally), because an expected $500,000 donor contribution failed to materialize. The scope is unchanged; TSS and the Chemical Division justify the increase. Funds for FY55 are set aside but TSS lacks the extra $250,000, which can be obligated by year-end.

title: AMENDMENT TO SUBPROJECT 35, PROJECT MKULTRA

nodes.title: I. Background of Subproject 35.
nodes.summary: Amendment to Subproject 35 of Project MKULTRA, approved by the DCI in January 1955, establishing a cover organization for sensitive biological, chemical, and radiological warfare research by DD/P/TSS's Chemical Division. The Agency covertly funds construction of a new research wing via a cut-out so the university and hospital remain unaware of Agency participation. Future projects would use the facility and be funded separately. Background and OGC comments are attached as tabs.

nodes.title: II. Building Fund.
nodes.summary: Describes a $3,000,000 Building Fund for a six-story hospital addition (land, heating, and power excluded, provided by the University). Public Law 221 matches University funds. Subproject 35 plan: University allocates $1,000,000 and takes upkeep/staffing; Fund donates $250,000 (including a $125,000 Agency grant); $500,000 from another agency for radiological research in the new wing; $1,250,000 matched under Public Law 221. CIA contribution inflates the federal share, justified for security.

nodes.title: III
nodes.summary: OCR-garbled excerpt describing an original informal commitment, first made through verbal discussions and correspondence, that was later changed by a policy decision. The DCI and a subordinate were preoccupied with a controversy, so the commitment shifted from contributing to the building fund to an annual research program of about $50,000 to $75,000. Whether the change was suggested by others or originated with one party is unknown. Once the change became apparent, additional funds were needed to complete the hospital construction.

nodes.title: IV. Suggcsted Funding.
nodes.summary: Proposes funding the $3,000,000 hospital wing: $1,000,000 from a donation (including $375,000 supplied by CIA), $500,000 from another source, and $1,500,000 in matched funds under Public Law 221. Explains Subproject 35's amendment to contribute an additional $250,000 to the building fund, raising its total from $125,000 to $375,000, while total Government contribution stays at $1,875,000. Notes the increase is not unusual in magnitude, and that the original contribution was not yet transmitted and payment is conditioned on adequate funds being made available, as specified by the DCI.

nodes.title: V. Source of CIA Funds.
nodes.summary: Describes the source of CIA funds for a project: the initially approved $125,000 was segregated within the TSS FY 1955 Research and Development budget. Insufficient funds remain for an additional $230,000 supplementary sum, so the TSS budget is requested to increase by that amount, to be made available to Subproject 35 of Project MKULTRA. Document is copy 1 of 1, page 3 of a numbered series.

nodes.title: VI. Comments by the Office of General Counsel.
nodes.summary: Comments by the Office of General Counsel. Tab 3 is a December 21, 1954 memorandum from the General Counsel to the DCI, commenting on Subproject 35: no fundamental legal objections if probable benefits are considered a fair return for the expenditure. The amendment to the Subproject only increases funds and changes no other aspect of the project. The project was referred back to the OGC though no structural change is contemplated; Tab 4 contains his comments.

nodes.title: VII. Justification.
nodes.summary: Describes a CIA contribution of $375,000 to a TSS hospital-wing project and its justification: one-sixth of new wing space for the Chemical Division (labs, offices, animals), deniable sponsorship of sensitive research, professional cover for three biochemical staff, and controlled access to human volunteers. Notes Subproject 35 origins (1954), accelerated occupancy (months rather than 18+ months) via a non-profit fund raising $500,000, security coordination, unchanged agreements, and financial savings from avoiding overhead charges matched by equal Public Law 221 funds.

nodes.title: Security and Agreement Terms for TSS Funding and Cover Arrangements
nodes.summary: The page notes that the expected 18-month wait for TSS facilities has been overcome: IMVJW raised the $500,000 for his Fund and may use existing hospital space to build the organization that will later occupy the new wing, so TSS can start using the cover within months. Section VIII says security details are being coordinated with the TSS Liaison and Security Officer, and fund transmittal and cover arrangements are in Tab A, unchanged. Section IX says the agreement, his co-operation, and control over his actions are unchanged and described in Tab A.

nodes.title: X. Resultant Financial Saving.
nodes.summary: Describes a CIA-funded cover facility under Project MKULTRA (Subproject 35) for covert biological, chemical, and radiological warfare research. The CIA contributes $375,000, matched by $375,000 in Public Law 221 funds, leaving total federal funds unchanged. The facility avoids the roughly 80% overhead normally charged on openly sponsored government research, letting the Agency buy more research. It also provides cover and security unobtainable elsewhere, and the text notes no legal objection was found.

nodes.title: I. Background of Project MKULTRA.
nodes.summary: Describes Project MKULTRA, approved by the DCI in 1953, which let TSS conduct sensitive research without signed contracts, preserving secrecy and protecting scientists' reputations. It covers audit provisions, file retention by TSS, and the use of a research fund as cut-out and prime contractor, including chemical/biological warfare work since 1951. It also profiles a Fund director and board member with Navy research ties, and a planned six-story clinical research wing funded by fund-raising.

nodes.title: Incorporated Fund's Background: Basic Research and Board Members
nodes.summary: Section II describes a six-member Board of Directors, one of whom serves as Executive Director. The Fund was incorporated to finance basic research in chemotherapy of cancer, asthma, hypertension, psychosomatic disorders, and other chronic diseases, and has solicited funds from various individuals. Since 1951 it has worked with the Chemical Division, acting as a cut-out for contractors in covert chemical and biological warfare and as a prime contractor for biological research. Current Agency projects follow previously approved controls. Section III describes a board member, internationally known in pharmacology research, with wartime Navy service and a continuing Navy medical research consulting role. He and two other board members are top secret cleared and aware of Agency sponsorship.

nodes.title: IV.
nodes.summary: Describes a university fund-raising campaign to build a new six-story clinical research wing (320 ft long, 50 ft wide) on an existing building. Two-thirds of the space will be research laboratories and offices, with 100 research beds in the remainder. The effort is backed by the medical faculty and University officers, who have advanced preliminary arrangements. Participation in the campaign would give the participant control of one-sixth of the total space, in addition to base and general out-patient facilities.

nodes.title: V. Financial Situation.
nodes.summary: Describes a University building project needing about $3,000,000 (excluding land and heating/power already available). Public Law 221 matches University-raised funds; the University allocated $1,000,000 and will handle upkeep and staffing. A CIA grant of $125,000 (valued at $250,000 with a matching donation) is conditional on refund if construction does not proceed. A $500,000 donation is encouraged for the new wing. Federal contribution of $1,250,000 includes the CIA share, which helps maintain security.

nodes.title: VI. Difficulties Faced by TSS.
nodes.summary: Describes difficulties faced by TSS Chemical Division in covert biological, chemical, and radiological warfare research due to lacking cover. Project MKULTRA gives administrative and financial cover but not personnel cover, and its future use is limited by growing numbers of cleared staff aware of Agency ties, lack of cover exposing contacts to personal risk, and intra-Agency awareness of the Fund's relationship. Career planning for technical and scientific biological personnel is also hindered. A proposed research-facility hospital wing subproject could integrate up to three Chemical Division employees, providing cover and easing dangerous conditions.

nodes.title: VII. 'Advantages and Benefits Accruing to TSS.
nodes.summary: Describes advantages to TSS's Chemical Division from a university research arrangement: one-sixth of a new research wing space and staff/equipment/animals provided; projects funded individually via Project MKULTRA with its controls; deniable Agency sponsorship; professional cover for three biochemical employees to attend scientific meetings; access to human volunteers under clinical supervision; a hospital safehouse; improved research output; recruiting via the Graduate School; and use of the university library and reprint service.

nodes.title: VIII. Funding.
nodes.summary: Proposal to grant $125,000 from the FY 1955 TSS Research and Development budget under MKULTRA procedures, matched by an equal Agency amount for a total $250,000 donation to a university's new hospital wing ($3,000,000 construction goal). The grant is a single, non-recurring contribution with no residual Agency interest in the building or equipment. Funds go through established cover channels, and the university remains unaware of Agency sponsorship. Future sensitive TSS projects will be financed individually through the annual R&D budget. Project activities continue unaffected if a named individual dies.

nodes.title: IX. Memorandum of Agreement.
nodes.summary: Describes a memorandum of agreement under which hospital space controlled by the signer will be made available to Chemical Division personnel, specifying cover arrangements and other benefits. No contract will be signed because it could not reflect the Agency's contractual terms. The signer makes arrangements with the University for the donation in question, and the memorandum is retained in TSS.

nodes.title: XI. Resultant Financial Saving.
nodes.summary: Explains the financial saving from using a non-profit cut-out. The $125,000 CIA contribution plus $125,000 in matching funds under P.L. 221 to the Building Fund will be more than offset within a few years. When the government sponsors research directly at a university or educational institution, it customarily pays salaries, equipment, supplies, and overhead, with overhead about 80% of salaries. When it sponsors research through a non-profit foundation, funds cover salaries, equipment, and supplies but not overhead, so the government dollar buys considerably more research.

summary: Amendment to Subproject 35 of Project MKULTRA (approved 1955) funds a covert CIA cover facility for chemical, biological, and radiological warfare research by TSS's Chemical Division, via a non-profit Building Fund that finances a six-story university hospital research wing unaware of Agency involvement. Funding totals $3,000,000: University $1,000,000, Fund donations (CIA share raised from $125,000 to $375,000), $500,000 from another agency, and Public Law 221 matching funds, leaving total federal funds unchanged. Justifications include one-sixth of wing space, deniable sponsorship, professional cover for staff, access to volunteers, faster occupancy, and savings from avoiding ~80% overhead. OGC found no fundamental legal objection; security and agreement terms are coordinated and unchanged.

title: MEMORANDUM FOR: THE RECORD
summary: A 1963 CIA-style trip report on arranging project close-out before the 30 June fiscal deadline: funds cannot carry over, so work was limited to 26 cases (13 completed, 4 transcribed, 8 in progress), with a final visit set for 16 June and a balance statement due within 10 days. The investigator notes the project lead focused on administrative problems, not results, and discusses his talk on delays and requests for more funding. A 1958 letter closes a drug experiment on releasing guarded information: 25 of 30 cases used, with abstracts, transcripts, intelligence tests, and a final financial accounting enclosed, plus an explanation of extra compensation to one doctor and a final $1356.26 check.

nodes.title: C. TECHNICAL PROGRESS
nodes.summary: A 1950s-era report on brain concussion research. It covers technical progress: fluid-filled glass skull acceleration thresholds, pressure fluctuation data from impact or airborne sound, and cavitation pattern studies. It notes the immersion blast study was deferred, reports November billing of $4,034.61, and requests continued funding. It then discusses concussion-inducing methods: impact devices, blast waves, tuned drivers, and sound fields, including their covert use in brainwashing. It closes with a proposed gas-bubble spinal technique to give temporary immunity.

Covers MKULTRA subprojects run by TSD. Subproject 45 continuations (1950s-1977) fund synthesis and clinical evaluation of psychochemical, 'knockout', and stressor compounds, with budget caps, audit, and fund-return conditions. Subproject 149 funds field tests of delivery systems with a businessman ($10,000). A 1956 request funds brain concussion research based on resonance-cavitation theory ($24,925). title: MATERIAL FOR THE RECORD
summary: MKSEARCH was the post-MKULTRA continuation (funded FY1966-FY1972) to develop covert biological, chemical, and radioactive methods for predictable human behavioral or physiological changes. From 1967, ORD and Edgewood Arsenal ran a drug-research program with two projects: OFTEN (animal and human toxicological and behavioral testing) and CHICKWIT (acquiring foreign drug developments and samples). DOD and CIA disagree on who financed and sponsored June 1973 human testing at Edgewood.

title: THE DIRECTOR OF CENTRAL. INTELLIGENCE
summary: A 23 December 1977 letter from DCI Office of Legislative Counsel to Senator Daniel Inouye, Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. It responds to Admiral Turner's 3 August 1977 testimony asking whether any Agency employees were terminated for participating in MKULTRA Subproject 3. Agency records were searched and confirmed that no such terminations occurred.

title: QKHILLTOP DEFINITION
summary: QKHILLTOP was a 1954 cryptonym for a project studying Chinese Communist brainwashing and developing interrogation techniques. Most early studies were conducted by the Cornell University Medical School Huipan Ecology Study Programs. The effort was absorbed into the MKULTRA program, making the cryptonym obsolete. The Society for the Investigation of Human Ecology, later the Human Ecology Fund, grew out of QKHILLTOP.
